materials.review_notes: Conspicuous fine grid/striated repetition reads as patterned surfacing rather than quiet structural concrete. Stronger alternatives exist in the same review set.

Strong cast/formwork concrete with credible tie holes and panel joints. Good structural-language material, but strongly dependent on element size and composition. Prefer small/medium structural spans, beams, columns, reveals, ceiling areas, or wall areas whose composition breaks repetition. Do not assume it is appropriate for a very large uninterrupted wall with most of its surface exposed; room-level review must confirm repetition remains acceptable.
Clean restrained cinder-block material. Useful as a historical construction layer or secondary wall language.

At 3.0 m/repeat the reinforced-slab/formwork language reads at a credible structural scale. Strong horizontal seams/tie-hole rhythm make this a secondary or deliberately composed structural material rather than a universal wall treatment.

One of the strongest current candidates. Rough mottled concrete with useful variation and no dominant square-tile pattern in the current review. Approved for service floors and also for walls where its scale/pattern fits the structural composition. Later EAF4 joints, repairs, drainage, markings, and wear should provide room-scale history rather than baking all variation into the source material.
Very quiet light concrete floor candidate. Useful control/low-noise option for Receiving-scale comparison.
Useful warmer mineral counterpart to ConcreteGrey; quiet enough for large structural surfaces.
Technically readable but extremely busy with repeated trowel/scratch/marking detail. Better held for a specific rough repair/unfinished context than promoted as a general applied finish.

Useful lighter rough structural concrete. The larger repeat and reduced normal strength make the broad mottling substantially calmer than the initial configuration. It responds well to Receiving Target lighting and provides a useful light-value structural option. Room-level review should still check repetition on very large uninterrupted surfaces.
Good darker/cooler concrete option with broad mineral variation. It becomes substantially darker under Receiving lighting, so room-level use should be bounded.
Dominant regular square-joint pattern reads as repeated concrete tile/panel flooring, conflicting with the VDD direction to avoid one obvious repeating concrete tile as the dominant floor solution.
Regular square/panel boundaries and strong pitting dominate the floor read, conflicting with the goal of avoiding one obvious repeating concrete-tile solution.
Credible light formed/panel concrete. Strong joint rhythm makes it better for bounded wall/structural uses than as an automatic whole-room surface.
Quiet rough concrete floor with useful fine surface texture and little baked directional wear.
Subtle dusty/warm concrete floor. The wear signal is broad enough to function as baseline substrate rather than a repeated localized decal; later EAF4 wear should remain restrained.
Strong bright rough-panel candidate for secondary structure, reveals and bounded wall fields. Explicit horizontal seams should remain compositionally deliberate.
Strong quiet grey floor candidate; enough mineral variation to avoid sterility without a dominant geometric motif.
Strong repeated pale scuff/mark motif bakes localized wear into every repeat and dominates at room scale. EAF4 should own localized wear.
Strong shuttered/formwork concrete language. Horizontal construction lines are readable but credible; later Receiving-scale review should control repetition/orientation.
Useful light-value structural concrete. Broad variation stays restrained enough for large surfaces and remains legible under Receiving lighting.

The calibrated value produces a restrained pale render/plaster with low visual noise. Approve as an applied wall finish; room-level composition will decide whether it adds anything over similar pale finishes.
Strong quiet medium/dark concrete with restrained variation and no dominant baked wear motif.

Useful pale aged cement/render finish. The reduced normal strength and larger repeat calm the initial fibrous read enough for localized wall-finish use. It should remain an applied finish over older structural substrate rather than defining the whole bunker shell. Its broad mottling already supplies some baseline age, so later EAF4 wear should remain restrained.

The reduced albedo reveals a useful aged painted/mineral wall finish with readable trowel/patch history. Approve as an applied finish, not structural substrate. Use in deliberate bounded regions; the repeated repair/paint history is too assertive for automatic whole-room coverage.
Potential older/dirtier plaster for later spaces, but its baked dark/streaked character risks taking over work intended for EAF4 wear and surface history.
Dense cracking, scratches and high-frequency surface breakup dominate at review scale and duplicate history that EAF4 should place locally.
Useful darker industrial floor with broad low-frequency variation. Room-level review should confirm it does not become too warm/dark under Receiving lighting.
Potential secondary/darker structural family, but currently less useful than the selected and rerun candidates. Revisit only if a later room needs this darker regular language.
At 0.70 albedo the stucco remains a light finish without overwhelming the review rig. Broad soft mottling is restrained enough for localized institutional/rendered wall finish.
Severe macro block/repeat structure and excessive brightness make large surfaces visibly tiled and unsuitable for the desired quiet mineral shell.
Restrained worn floor with broad, low-amplitude history. Quiet enough to retain as a service-floor option.

Strong medium/darker rough concrete option with restrained pitting and broad tonal variation. Useful as an older/rougher structural counterpart to the brighter concrete and formed concrete. Under Receiving lighting it becomes substantially darker, so room-level composition should avoid using it as the only dominant shell material where readability would suffer.
The calibrated value exposes a quiet pale plaster/concrete finish with subtle vertical mineral variation. Useful as a restrained Layer-2 wall finish.
Useful large concrete-block/panel secondary with readable tie-hole/construction character. Strong grid means bounded use rather than default shell coverage.
Quiet, fine-grained mineral surface with good response under both rigs. Despite the source name, the reviewed surface does not bake dominant grime/damage into the material.
Technically convincing, but large weathered/peeled areas dominate the surface history. Better reserved for rougher/less-maintained spaces than the Receiving baseline.
Blockwork itself is useful but this variant carries substantial dark staining/grime across every repeat. Defer behind cleaner masonry options.
Excellent low-noise structural candidate. Broad mottling remains calm and gives later architecture, loot and services visual bandwidth.

Potential localized damaged/repair finish, not a preferred baseline render. Also retains the unsupported Substance-graph warning. Revisit only if later EAF4/EAF5 work needs this specific damaged-finish language.

Reduced albedo makes the concrete panel/block language readable without clipping. Useful as secondary masonry/panel construction; visible panel rhythm should remain bounded and architecturally deliberate.

Reduced albedo resolves the clipping and reveals convincing large staggered concrete blockwork. Strong block rhythm makes it best suited to secondary/historical construction fields rather than default whole-room coverage.
Valid concrete source but comparatively busy/high-contrast with repeated patch/board-like variation. Keep available for later context rather than prioritizing it for Receiving.
Strong restrained service-floor candidate with quiet warm mineral variation and no dominant tile grid.
